claim: Enzalutamide prolongs survival for patients with metastatic CRPC.
source: Enzalutamide is a potent next-generation AR antagonist and prolongs survival for patients with metastatic CRPC (Beer et al., 2014; Scher et al., 2012; Tran et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Beer et al., 2014; Scher et al., 2012; Tran et al., 2009).

claim: Enzalutamide resistance almost always emerges, eventually leading to disease lethality.
source: Unfortunately, enzalutamide resistance almost always emerges, eventually leading to disease lethality.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge about enzalutamide resistance in prostate cancer.

claim: Potent AR inhibition with enzalutamide leads to a massive up-regulation of GR expression.
source: Emerging data suggest that potent AR inhibition with enzalutamide leads to a massive up-regulation of GR expression, which then permits the re-expression of about 50% of AR-responsive genes, in turn promoting tumor progression (Arora et al., 2013; Isikbay et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Arora et al., 2013; Isikbay et al., 2014).

claim: GR up-regulation permits the re-expression of about 50% of AR-responsive genes.
source: Emerging data suggest that potent AR inhibition with enzalutamide leads to a massive up-regulation of GR expression, which then permits the re-expression of about 50% of AR-responsive genes, in turn promoting tumor progression (Arora et al., 2013; Isikbay et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Arora et al., 2013; Isikbay et al., 2014).

claim: Total and systemic GR blockade is incompatible with life.
source: Furthermore, targeting such a mechanism with GR antagonists may be problematic because total and systemic GR blockade is incompatible with life (Sharifi, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Sharifi, 2014).

claim: 11β-HSD2 enzymatically converts cortisol to inactive cortisone in humans.
source: GR stimulation by cortisol in peripheral tissues is physiologically tightly regulated by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-2 (11β-HSD2), which enzymatically converts cortisol to inactive cortisone in humans and corticosterone to 11-dehydrocorticosterone in mice (Figure 1A) (Chapman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Chapman et al., 2013) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: 11β-HSD2 converts corticosterone to 11-dehydrocorticosterone in mice.
source: GR stimulation by cortisol in peripheral tissues is physiologically tightly regulated by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-2 (11β-HSD2), which enzymatically converts cortisol to inactive cortisone in humans and corticosterone to 11-dehydrocorticosterone in mice (Figure 1A) (Chapman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Chapman et al., 2013) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Fetal and placental 11β-HSD2 expression shields against maternal cortisol.
source: For example, fetal and placental 11β-HSD2 expression shields against maternal cortisol, thereby restricting GR stimulation and blocking premature fetal maturation (Chapman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Chapman et al., 2013).

claim: Long but not short (i.e., 24 hr) enzalutamide exposure sustains cortisol levels by retarding conversion to cortisone in cells and media.
source: Long but not short (i.e., 24 hr) enzalutamide exposure sustains cortisol levels by retarding conversion to cortisone in cells and media (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Freshly harvested CRPC xenograft tumors treated with enzalutamide have an impaired capability of inactivating [3H]-cortisol by conversion to cortisone.
source: Similarly, freshly harvested CRPC xenograft tumors grown in orchiectomized mice and treated with enzalutamide (Tran et al., 2009) have an impaired capability of inactivating [3H]-cortisol by conversion to cortisone, when compared to tumors from mice treated with orchiectomy alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and a citation (Tran et al., 2009).

claim: Enzalutamide suppresses LAPC4 viability in vitro.
source: Enzalutamide suppresses LAPC4 viability in vitro (Figure 1D) in association with suppression of AR-regulated genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Enzalutamide suppresses AR-regulated genes.
source: Enzalutamide suppresses LAPC4 viability in vitro (Figure 1D) in association with suppression of AR-regulated genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Growth recovers after sustained enzalutamide treatment.
source: Growth recovers after sustained enzalutamide treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of 11β-HSD2 protein in AR-expressing LAPC4, VCaP and MDA-PCa-2b prostate cancer cell lines was observed with enzalutamide treatment.
source: Loss of 11β-HSD2 protein in AR-expressing LAPC4, VCaP and MDA-PCa-2b prostate cancer cell lines (but not an AR-negative prostate cancer cell line [Figure 2—figure supplement 1A]) was observed with enzalutamide treatment, while no consistent effect on 11β-HSD1 was detectable (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Enzalutamide treatment does not cause loss of 11β-HSD2 protein in an AR-negative prostate cancer cell line.
source: Loss of 11β-HSD2 protein in AR-expressing LAPC4, VCaP and MDA-PCa-2b prostate cancer cell lines (but not an AR-negative prostate cancer cell line [Figure 2—figure supplement 1A]) was observed with enzalutamide treatment, while no consistent effect on 11β-HSD1 was detectable (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No consistent effect on 11β-HSD1 was detectable with enzalutamide treatment.
source: Loss of 11β-HSD2 protein in AR-expressing LAPC4, VCaP and MDA-PCa-2b prostate cancer cell lines (but not an AR-negative prostate cancer cell line [Figure 2—figure supplement 1A]) was observed with enzalutamide treatment, while no consistent effect on 11β-HSD1 was detectable (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No suppression of HSD11B2 mRNA was observed with enzalutamide treatment.
source: No suppression of HSD11B2 mRNA, which encodes 11β-HSD2, was observed with enzalutamide treatment, suggesting that 11β-HSD2 protein loss is not attributable to transcriptional suppression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and no direct 11β-HSD2 antagonism by enzalutamide was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 11β-HSD2 protein loss is not attributable to transcriptional suppression.
source: No suppression of HSD11B2 mRNA, which encodes 11β-HSD2, was observed with enzalutamide treatment, suggesting that 11β-HSD2 protein loss is not attributable to transcriptional suppression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and no direct 11β-HSD2 antagonism by enzalutamide was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HSD11B2 mRNA is not suppressed, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No direct 11β-HSD2 antagonism by enzalutamide was observed.
source: No suppression of HSD11B2 mRNA, which encodes 11β-HSD2, was observed with enzalutamide treatment, suggesting that 11β-HSD2 protein loss is not attributable to transcriptional suppression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and no direct 11β-HSD2 antagonism by enzalutamide was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 11β-HSD2 loss is not attributable to GR stimulation.
source: Importantly, 11β-HSD2 loss is not attributable to GR stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Nine of 11 tissues treated with enzalutamide obtained from patients with prostate cancer had a loss of 11β-HSD2 with treatment.
source: Nine of 11 tissues treated with enzalutamide obtained from patients with prostate cancer (two metastatic CRPC, two local prostate tissues from patients treated neoadjuvantly with enzalutamide and seven fresh tissues treated with enzalutamide ex vivo) had a loss of 11β-HSD2 with treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patient tissues shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GR up-regulation was observed in a subset of clinical tissues.
source: Consistent with previously published observations (Arora et al., 2013), GR up-regulation was observed in a subset of clinical tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), all of which had 11β-HSD2 loss in Figure 2E.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and a citation (Arora et al., 2013).

claim: All tissues that had GR up-regulation also exhibited 11β-HSD2 loss.
source: Consistent with previously published observations (Arora et al., 2013), GR up-regulation was observed in a subset of clinical tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), all of which had 11β-HSD2 loss in Figure 2E.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: 11β-HSD2 reinstatement with both stable expression and transient transfection studies reverted the glucocorticoid metabolic phenotype of enzalutamide treated cells back to rapid cortisol inactivation.
source: 11β-HSD2 reinstatement with both stable expression and transient transfection studies reverted the glucocorticoid metabolic phenotype of enzalutamide treated cells back to rapid cortisol inactivation that is characteristic of enzalutamide-naïve cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of 11β-HSD2 replacement are specific to glucocorticoid substrates of 11β-HSD2 (i.e., cortisol but not dexamethasone) and GR-responsive genes (i.e., PSA and KLF9).
source: Furthermore, the effects of 11β-HSD2 replacement on transcription of PSA (Figure 3C), which is regulated by AR and GR, KLF9, which is regulated by GR only and PMEPA1, which is regulated by AR only (Arora et al., 2013), suggest that the effects are indeed specific to glucocorticoid substrates of 11β-HSD2 (i.e., cortisol but not dexamethasone) and GR-responsive genes (i.e., PSA and KLF9).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and a citation (Arora et al., 2013).

claim: Forced 11β-HSD2 expression significantly reversed enzalutamide-resistant growth and prolonged progression-free survival in LAPC4 xenografts.
source: Tumors appeared to harbor significant resistance to treatment with enzalutamide, as evidenced by the growth of Vector xenografts through enzalutamide therapy. Forced 11β-HSD2 expression significantly reversed enzalutamide-resistant growth and prolonged progression-free survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: 11β-HSD2 expression had no significant effect on untreated tumors.
source: In contrast, 11β-HSD2 expression had no significant effect on untreated tumors, supporting a model in which the effect of 11β-HSD2 on tumor growth is specific to the context of resistance to potent AR antagonist therapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Reinstatement of sensitivity to enzalutamide treatment also occurred in a second (VCaP) xenograft model of CRPC.
source: Reinstatement of sensitivity to enzalutamide treatment also occurred in a second (VCaP) xenograft model of CRPC (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C–D.

claim: 11β-HSD2 reinstatement depleted corticosterone concentrations by approximately two-thirds in enzalutamide-treated tumors (44.5 pmol/g in vector tumors vs. 15.1 pmol/g in 11β-HSD2 tumors; p=0.002).
source: 11β-HSD2 reinstatement depleted corticosterone concentrations by approximately two-thirds in enzalutamide-treated tumors (44.5 pmol/g in vector tumors vs. 15.1 pmol/g in 11β-HSD2 tumors; p=0.002), which otherwise harbor the capacity to metabolically sustain elevated concentrations of biologically active glucocorticoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Tumor 11β-HSD2 expression results in a significant decline in the percentage of tumor corticosterone (59% in vector tumors vs. 33% in 11β-HSD2 tumors; p<0.0001).
source: Tumor 11β-HSD2 expression also results in a significant decline in the percentage of tumor corticosterone (59% in vector tumors vs. 33% in 11β-HSD2 tumors; p<0.0001) when compared to the sum total of corticosterone plus 11-dehydrocorticosterone (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There is no significant change in serum in the absolute concentration of corticosterone (873 pmol/ml in vector mice vs. 867 pmol/ml in 11β-HSD2 mice; p=0.49) with 11β-HSD2 expression in enzalutamide treated mice.
source: In contrast to the effects of 11β-HSD2 expression on tumor glucocorticoids in enzalutamide treated mice, there is no significant change in serum in the absolute concentration (873 pmol/ml in vector mice vs. 867 pmol/ml in 11β-HSD2 mice; p=0.49; Figure 4G) or percentage of corticosterone (99.87% in vector mice vs. 99.85% in 11β-HSD2 mice; p<0.93; Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There is no significant change in serum in the percentage of corticosterone (99.87% in vector mice vs. 99.85% in 11β-HSD2 mice; p<0.93) with 11β-HSD2 expression in enzalutamide treated mice.
source: In contrast to the effects of 11β-HSD2 expression on tumor glucocorticoids in enzalutamide treated mice, there is no significant change in serum in the absolute concentration (873 pmol/ml in vector mice vs. 867 pmol/ml in 11β-HSD2 mice; p=0.49; Figure 4G) or percentage of corticosterone (99.87% in vector mice vs. 99.85% in 11β-HSD2 mice; p<0.93; Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A physical association between 11β-HSD2 and AMFR is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: A physical association between 11β-HSD2 and AMFR is supported by immunoprecipitation of AMFR, followed by immunoblot for 11β-HSD2, as well as immunoprecipitation of 11β-HSD2, followed by immunoblot for AMFR (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of 11β-HSD2, Ubiquitin-His, and AMFR-Myc-DDK, followed by Ni-agarose pull-down and anti-11β-HSD2 immunoblot demonstrates the AMFR-dependence of 11β-HSD2 ubiquitination.
source: Expression of 11β-HSD2, Ubiquitin-His, and AMFR-Myc-DDK, followed by Ni-agarose pull-down and anti-11β-HSD2 immunoblot demonstrates the AMFR-dependence of 11β-HSD2 ubiquitination (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Enzalutamide treatment did not consistently increase AMFR expression.
source: Enzalutamide treatment did not consistently increase AMFR expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Erlin-2 was more consistently up-regulated with enzalutamide treatment, including in 8 of 11 patient tissues.
source: However, Erlin-2, which enables the AMFR-associated endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation pathway (ERAD), was more consistently up-regulated, including in 8 of 11 patient tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) (Browman et al., 2006; Pearce et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C and citations (Browman et al., 2006; Pearce et al., 2007).

claim: Genetically silencing AMFR with stable shRNA expression promotes an increase in 11β-HSD2 protein.
source: The functional consequence of 11β-HSD2 / AMFR interaction and 11β-HSD2 ubiquitination is evidenced by genetically silencing AMFR with stable shRNA expression, which promotes an increase in 11β-HSD2 protein (Figure 5C) but not transcript (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genetically silencing AMFR does not increase 11β-HSD2 transcript.
source: The functional consequence of 11β-HSD2 / AMFR interaction and 11β-HSD2 ubiquitination is evidenced by genetically silencing AMFR with stable shRNA expression, which promotes an increase in 11β-HSD2 protein (Figure 5C) but not transcript (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The enzalutamide-induced metabolic phenotype that sustains cortisol concentrations by way of retarded inactivation is reversed with genetic ablation of AMFR.
source: Furthermore, the enzalutamide-induced metabolic phenotype that sustains cortisol concentrations by way of retarded inactivation is reversed with genetic ablation of AMFR (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Silencing both 11β-HSD2 and AMFR with enzalutamide treatment negates the effect of genetically silencing AMFR alone.
source: Silencing both 11β-HSD2 and AMFR with enzalutamide treatment negates the effect of genetically silencing AMFR alone, suggesting that the effect of AMFR is mediated through 11β-HSD2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The effect of AMFR is mediated through 11β-HSD2.
source: Silencing both 11β-HSD2 and AMFR with enzalutamide treatment negates the effect of genetically silencing AMFR alone, suggesting that the effect of AMFR is mediated through 11β-HSD2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that silencing both 11β-HSD2 and AMFR negates the effect of AMFR silencing alone, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Stable AMFR knockdown suppressed xenograft growth and prolonged progression-free survival in enzalutamide-treated xenografts.
source: Finally, the functional relevance and requirement for AMFR expression on enzalutamide resistance is suggested by suppressed xenograft growth and prolonged progression-free survival in enzalutamide-treated xenografts with stable AMFR knockdown (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E–F.

claim: Tumors with AMFR knockdown were confirmed to have sustained 11β-HSD2 protein expression.
source: Tumors with AMFR knockdown were confirmed to have sustained 11β-HSD2 protein expression, thus impairing enzalutamide resistance (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Metastatic prostate cancer usually responds initially to medical or surgical castration, then eventually progresses as castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC).
source: Metastatic prostate cancer usually responds initially to medical or surgical castration, then eventually progresses as castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which is stimulated by intratumoral synthesis of testosterone and/or 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and activation of the androgen receptor (AR) (Attard et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2013; Mostaghel et al., 2014; Scher and Sawyers, 2005; Hearn et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Attard et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2013; Mostaghel et al., 2014; Scher and Sawyers, 2005; Hearn et al., 2016).

claim: CRPC is stimulated by intratumoral synthesis of testosterone and/or 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and activation of the androgen receptor (AR).
source: Metastatic prostate cancer usually responds initially to medical or surgical castration, then eventually progresses as castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which is stimulated by intratumoral synthesis of testosterone and/or 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and activation of the androgen receptor (AR) (Attard et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2013; Mostaghel et al., 2014; Scher and Sawyers, 2005; Hearn et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Attard et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2013; Mostaghel et al., 2014; Scher and Sawyers, 2005; Hearn et al., 2016).

claim: Enzalutamide is a potent next-generation AR antagonist.
source: Enzalutamide is a potent next-generation AR antagonist and prolongs survival for patients with metastatic CRPC (Beer et al., 2014; Scher et al., 2012; Tran et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Beer et al., 2014; Scher et al., 2012; Tran et al., 2009).

claim: Enzalutamide treatment in human models of prostate cancer and patient tissues is accompanied by AMFR mediating loss of 11β-HSD2.
source: We show that enzalutamide treatment in human models of prostate cancer and patient tissues is accompanied by a ubiquitin E3-ligase, AMFR, mediating loss of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-2 (11β-HSD2), which otherwise inactivates cortisol, sustaining tumor cortisol concentrations to stimulate GR and enzalutamide resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: 11β-HSD2 otherwise inactivates cortisol.
source: We show that enzalutamide treatment in human models of prostate cancer and patient tissues is accompanied by a ubiquitin E3-ligase, AMFR, mediating loss of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-2 (11β-HSD2), which otherwise inactivates cortisol, sustaining tumor cortisol concentrations to stimulate GR and enzalutamide resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about 11β-HSD2 function.

claim: Loss of 11β-HSD2 sustains tumor cortisol concentrations to stimulate GR and enzalutamide resistance.
source: We show that enzalutamide treatment in human models of prostate cancer and patient tissues is accompanied by a ubiquitin E3-ligase, AMFR, mediating loss of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-2 (11β-HSD2), which otherwise inactivates cortisol, sustaining tumor cortisol concentrations to stimulate GR and enzalutamide resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Reinstatement of 11β-HSD2 expression reverses enzalutamide resistance in mouse xenograft tumors.
source: Remarkably, reinstatement of 11β-HSD2 expression, or AMFR loss, reverses enzalutamide resistance in mouse xenograft tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: AMFR loss reverses enzalutamide resistance in mouse xenograft tumors.
source: Remarkably, reinstatement of 11β-HSD2 expression, or AMFR loss, reverses enzalutamide resistance in mouse xenograft tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E–F.

claim: Enzalutamide resistance is marked by sustained cortisol concentrations in the prostate tumor that are attributable to a profound loss of 11β-HSD2 and impaired conversion to cortisone.
source: Here, we show that enzalutamide resistance is marked by sustained cortisol concentrations in the prostate tumor that are attributable to a profound loss of 11β-HSD2 and impaired conversion to cortisone, which together de-repress GR and stimulate glucocorticoid-dependent signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sustained cortisol concentrations and impaired conversion to cortisone de-repress GR and stimulate glucocorticoid-dependent signaling.
source: Here, we show that enzalutamide resistance is marked by sustained cortisol concentrations in the prostate tumor that are attributable to a profound loss of 11β-HSD2 and impaired conversion to cortisone, which together de-repress GR and stimulate glucocorticoid-dependent signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that 11β-HSD2 loss leads to sustained cortisol and GR stimulation.

claim: 11β-HSD2 loss is mediated by the ubiquitin E3-ligase autocrine mobility factor receptor (AMFR).
source: Mechanistically, 11β-HSD2 loss is mediated by the ubiquitin E3-ligase autocrine mobility factor receptor (AMFR).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sustained 11β-HSD2 expression reverses the metabolic phenotype of enzalutamide resistance and reinstates the therapeutic response to enzalutamide in vivo.
source: Finally, sustained 11β-HSD2 expression reverses the metabolic phenotype of enzalutamide resistance and reinstates the therapeutic response to enzalutamide in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Systemic availability of GR agonists represents only one aspect of tumor GR stimulation in the setting of enzalutamide resistance.
source: These findings indicate that systemic availability of GR agonists represents only one aspect of tumor GR stimulation in the setting of enzalutamide resistance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings that local metabolic regulation of cortisol by 11β-HSD2 is critical for GR stimulation.

claim: Local metabolic regulation of ligand availability by the tumor serves as a second critical aspect of tumor GR stimulation.
source: Local metabolic regulation of ligand availability by the tumor serves as a second critical aspect and can either oppose the effects of systemic glucocorticoids by spurring enzymatic inactivation, or instead allow unimpeded access to the tumor tissue, enabling sustained GR stimulation to promote tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings that 11β-HSD2 loss allows sustained cortisol levels in tumors.

claim: Glucocorticoid administration has long been recognized to have a therapeutic effect in CRPC.
source: Glucocorticoid administration has long been recognized to have a therapeutic effect in CRPC.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: The therapeutic effect of glucocorticoids is likely due in part to adrenal androgen suppression.
source: Although the therapeutic effect of glucocorticoids is likely due in part to adrenal androgen suppression, the complete effects of glucocorticoids in prostate cancer have yet to be fully elucidated (Attard et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Attard et al., 2012).

claim: Prednisolone is inactivated by 11β-HSD2 to prednisone.
source: For example, prednisolone is inactivated by 11β-HSD2 to prednisone but dexamethasone is generally thought to be impervious to inactivation by 11β-HSD2.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about glucocorticoid metabolism.

claim: Dexamethasone is generally thought to be impervious to inactivation by 11β-HSD2.
source: For example, prednisolone is inactivated by 11β-HSD2 to prednisone but dexamethasone is generally thought to be impervious to inactivation by 11β-HSD2.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about glucocorticoid metabolism.

claim: Baseline GR expression prior to enzalutamide treatment, where 11β-HSD2 expression is intact, may be associated with enzalutamide resistance.
source: This may be even more important prior to enzalutamide therapy and consequent suppression of 11β-HSD2 loss, because some data suggest that baseline GR expression prior to enzalutamide treatment, where 11β-HSD2 expression is intact, may be associated with enzalutamide resistance (Arora et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Arora et al., 2013).

claim: Early results from a neoadjuvant clinical trial of castration plus abiraterone suggest that tissue cortisol may be elevated specifically in prostate cancers that up-regulate GR.
source: Furthermore, early results from a neoadjuvant clinical trial of castration plus abiraterone suggest that tissue cortisol may be elevated specifically in prostate cancers that up-regulate GR (Efstathiou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Efstathiou et al., 2015).

claim: Altered tumor glucocorticoid metabolism by way of the mechanism elucidated occurs not only with enzalutamide but also with abiraterone therapy.
source: Thus, it is possible that altered tumor glucocorticoid metabolism by way of the mechanism we have elucidated occurs not only with enzalutamide but also with abiraterone therapy.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the findings with enzalutamide.

claim: Blocking 11β-HSD2 protein loss, for example by blocking AMFR, or reinstatement of 11β-HSD2 expression in the tumor may be an appropriate strategy to reverse enzalutamide resistance without affecting the systemic availability of glucocorticoids.
source: Our data raise the possibility that blocking 11β-HSD2 protein loss, for example by blocking AMFR, or reinstatement of 11β-HSD2 expression in the tumor may be an appropriate strategy to reverse enzalutamide resistance without affecting the systemic availability of glucocorticoids and resultant associated toxicities.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Blocking AMFR may also increase 3βHSD1 protein, sustaining androgen synthesis.
source: Blocking AMFR may also increase 3βHSD1 protein, sustaining androgen synthesis (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Chang et al., 2013).

claim: In the context of enzalutamide treatment, the net effect of AMFR ablation is therapeutic, probably because the AR ligand binding domain remains mainly occupied by enzalutamide and glucocorticoid signaling is a major driver of tumor progression.
source: However, our in vivo studies with AMFR knockdown suggest that in the context of enzalutamide treatment, the net effect of AMFR ablation is therapeutic, probably because the AR ligand binding domain remains mainly occupied by enzalutamide and glucocorticoid signaling is a major driver of tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5E–F.

claim: GR and AR have been implicated in a subtype-specific breast cancer progression.
source: For example, in addition to the involvement of GR in prostate cancer, GR and AR have been implicated in a subtype-specific breast cancer progression (Kach et al., 2015; Ni et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Kach et al., 2015; Ni et al., 2011).

claim: A switch in steroid receptors that drives disease processes more broadly may be accompanied by perturbed local metabolic regulation of the availability of ligands that stimulate steroid receptor activation.
source: Our results suggest that a switch in steroid receptors that drives disease processes more broadly may be accompanied by perturbed local metabolic regulation of the availability of ligands that stimulate steroid receptor activation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the findings in prostate cancer.

claim: The mouse adrenal does not express 17α-hydroxylase/17,20 lyase and thus synthesizes corticosterone instead of cortisol as the dominant glucocorticoid.
source: In contrast to humans, the mouse adrenal does not express 17α-hydroxylase/17,20 lyase and thus synthesizes corticosterone instead of cortisol as the dominant glucocorticoid (Figure 1A), which is similarly inactivated to 11-dehydrocorticosterone by 11β-HSD2 (Miller and Auchus, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Miller and Auchus, 2011) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Corticosterone is similarly inactivated to 11-dehydrocorticosterone by 11β-HSD2.
source: In contrast to humans, the mouse adrenal does not express 17α-hydroxylase/17,20 lyase and thus synthesizes corticosterone instead of cortisol as the dominant glucocorticoid (Figure 1A), which is similarly inactivated to 11-dehydrocorticosterone by 11β-HSD2 (Miller and Auchus, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Miller and Auchus, 2011) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: AMFR is a ubiquitin E3-ligase in the endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation pathway.
source: We previously described the role of AMFR, a ubiquitin E3-ligase in the endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation pathway, in regulation of another steroidogenic enzyme, 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-1 (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Chang et al., 2013).

claim: AMFR regulates 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-1.
